title: Gasoline Affordability and Unemployment
text:
Our main question is whether states with higher gasoline prices also have higher unemployment. Here, each point is a state in September 2026, colored by region. The x-axis is the real price of regular gasoline, and the y-axis is the unemployment rate. The gray line is a straight-line trend fitted across all 50 states, and the shaded band shows the uncertainty around it.








Figure 1: Real price of regular gasoline and unemployment rate, by state, September 2026. The gray line shows a straight-line trend, and the shaded band shows the uncertainty around it.




The trend line rises: states with more expensive gas tend to have somewhat higher unemployment, though the points are widely scattered around the line, so the relationship is weak. Because this compares states at a single point in time, it shows an association, not that higher gas prices cause higher unemployment.

title: Changes in Real Gasoline Prices
text:
To examine the geographical impact of the 2026 gasoline price crisis, we compare monthly average prices for regular gasoline across all 50 states between January and September 2026. We focus on this period because it encompasses the most substantial nationwide price increases observed in our dataset. All prices are expressed in September 2026 dollars per gallon, accounting for changes in the national consumer price index.

Each state is weighted equally when calculating regional averages, irrespective of its population or gasoline consumption. Standard deviation (SD), measured in percentage points (pp), indicates how much price increases varied among states within each region. A smaller standard deviation indicates more uniform price changes.
The gasoline price crisis of 2026 has affected the entire country. Between January and September, every state in the union experienced an increase in real regular gasoline prices, with the average state experiencing an increase of approximately 50.1%. However, the magnitude of these increases varied considerably. Utah experienced the largest increase at 73.9%, compared to Hawaii’s 19.9%. At the regional level, the Midwest led with a mean price increase of 53.5%, followed by the West (51.7%), the South (49.0%), and the Northeast (45.0%).
Notably, the Northeast experienced both the smallest and most uniform price increases, exhibiting the lowest regional mean and the smallest standard deviation of just 3.26 percentage points. No Northeastern state ranked among the ten largest price increases nationwide. Conversely, the West exhibited considerable variation, with a standard deviation of 15.56 percentage points, nearly five times that of the Northeast. The region contained the states with both the largest and smallest price increases, with six Western states ranking among the ten largest increases nationwide.

title: Changes in Real Gasoline Prices
text:
Explaining regional differences
The Northeast’s relatively uniform and moderate price increases may be attributable to several factors, including the geographical compactness of the region and the potential interconnectedness of its gasoline supply chains. Regional supply disruptions elsewhere may also have played a role. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (2026), refinery outages and maintenance in Illinois, Indiana, and Colorado contributed to elevated gasoline prices in the Midwest and Rocky Mountain regions during the spring of 2026.
Additionally, the Northeast entered 2026 with a relatively elevated average real gasoline price of $3.01 per gallon, compared to $2.72 in the Midwest and $2.71 in the South. Consequently, equivalent absolute price increases would translate into smaller percentage increases. While these factors may collectively help explain the observed regional differences, our analysis cannot establish a causal relationship.

title: Changes in Real Gasoline Prices
text:
Explore the data
The interactive table below allows readers to investigate real gasoline price changes across different states, regions, and time periods, extending beyond our analysis of 2026.
Use the filters at the top of the table to select states, regions, a start month, an end month, and price ranges. Leave the state filter blank to display all states in the selected regions. For a direct comparison across states, select exactly one start month and one end month. The end month must be later than the start month.
Click any column heading to sort the results.
Positive values indicate that gasoline became more expensive relative to the general consumer price level, while negative values indicate the opposite.

title: Changes in Real Gasoline Prices
text:
Limitations
January 2026 coincided with the lowest nationwide average real gasoline price observed in our dataset. Consequently, the magnitude of the reported increases is sensitive to our choice of starting month. Nevertheless, January provides a natural starting point for examining price changes during 2026.
Within the broader dataset, October 2025 is excluded because CPI data are unavailable in our source dataset. November 2024 contains only observations beginning November 16, while March and May 2026 each have three missing days. Consequently, the corresponding monthly averages may not perfectly represent prices across the entirety of those months.
Our inflation adjustment uses the national consumer price index rather than state-specific measures of consumer inflation. Moreover, our regional averages weight each state equally and therefore should not be interpreted as the average price increase experienced by individual consumers.
Finally, our analysis describes changes between selected endpoints rather than fluctuations throughout the intervening period.

Software and Resources
Our approach to data wrangling, statistical analysis, and visualization draws upon the methods introduced in Modern Data Science with R (Baumer et al. 2021).
Data wrangling and analysis were conducted in R using tidyverse. Visualizations were developed using ggplot2, plotly, sf, and maps. Interactive tables were constructed using DT.
The website was developed using Quarto.

title: Gasoline Affordability and Unemployment
text:
Rising gasoline prices hurt most when household budgets are already strained. To see whether states with weaker labor markets also faced the steepest affordability burden, we compare each state’s unemployment rate with the number of hours of work needed to buy 15 gallons of regular gasoline in September 2026.
Hours per fill-up combines real gasoline prices, real weekly earnings, and average weekly hours:
\[
\text{Hours per fill-up} = \frac{15 \times \text{real gas price}}{\text{real weekly earnings} / \text{weekly hours}}
\]
A higher value means gasoline is less affordable for a typical worker in that state.








Figure 1: Unemployment rate and hours of work needed to buy 15 gallons of regular gasoline, by state, September 2026. The line shows the fitted simple linear regression with a 95% confidence band.




Hover over any point to see the state and its values.

title: Gasoline Affordability and Unemployment
text:
Limitations


One month only. The analysis uses September 2026 so that each state is an independent observation. The relationship may differ in other months.
Correlation, not causation. The regression describes an association across states and cannot show that unemployment or region causes differences in affordability.
Average workers. Hours per fill-up uses each state’s average weekly earnings and hours. It does not reflect affordability for unemployed people or low-wage workers, who may be hit hardest.
Small sample. With 50 states, the model has limited power to detect weak relationships.

To see whether states with weaker labor markets also faced a heavier gasoline burden, we compare each state’s unemployment rate with the number of hours of work needed to buy 15 gallons of regular gasoline in September 2026. Each point is a state, colored by region, and the gray line is a straight-line trend fitted across all states, with a shaded band showing the uncertainty around it. The trend line stays fairly flat, suggesting little relationship between unemployment and gasoline affordability across states. Hover over any point to see the state and its values.
